opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I've never really thought of myself as one of those top-of-the-class, everything-comes-easily kind of students. When I look at the people around me, especially back in China, there were always classmates who were just incredibly sharp: they won the olympiad medals, they got the perfect scores, they seemed to absorb things instantly. I wasn't that person. My path was more like a series of somewhat lucky turns, plus a lot of just staying curious and not giving up on things I found interesting.

I think the way I understand it now is that academic achievement in the narrow sense, exams and rankings, measures one kind of ability. Research, especially in a field like AI that changes so fast, rewards something a bit different. It rewards taste, being willing to work on problems that aren't fashionable yet, and being comfortable being wrong for a long time. Some of the most brilliant students I knew were extremely good at solving well-defined problems, but research is mostly about figuring out what the problem even is.

So I don't really compare myself on that same axis anymore. Early on I definitely had some insecurity about it. When you go to a top PhD program, or later to a place like FAIR, you're surrounded by people who are, frankly, smarter than you in many ways. But over time I realized the comparison isn't that useful. What matters more is whether you have your own perspective, whether you can find the questions you genuinely care about and push on them consistently.

And I've been very fortunate with mentors and collaborators. A lot of what people might see as my "trajectory" is really the result of being in the right environment with the right people at the right time. I try to be honest about that luck rather than tell a story where it was all planned or all talent.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I've never thought of myself as one of those students. When I look back, I was never the top of my class, not in high school, not in college at Shanghai Jiao Tong, not even in grad school at UCSD. There were always people around me who were faster, who could solve a problem the moment they saw it, who seemed to just understand things without effort. I wasn't that person.

What I had, I think, was a kind of stubbornness. I'd pick something and stay with it longer than was reasonable. In my PhD I spent a long time on things that, by any sensible measure, weren't working. ResNeXt, for example, came out of a very simple question that I kept returning to, which was whether you could make the architecture cleaner and more uniform rather than more complicated. It wasn't a brilliant idea. It was just that I didn't let go of it.

So when I compare myself to the really exceptional students, I think the difference is that they optimize well. They know where the frontier is and they go straight there. My path has been much more about wandering, taking detours, sometimes working on things that were unfashionable at the time. ConvNeXt was a bit like that too. Everyone had moved to transformers and I was asking whether we had actually given convolutions a fair shot. That's not the move a top student makes. That's the move someone makes who is a little bit contrarian and a little bit slow.

I've come to think that's fine. Research isn't an exam. Being the smartest person in the room matters much less than being able to tolerate confusion for a long time, and to keep asking a question after other people have decided it's already answered. If I have any advice for students who feel like they're not the brightest, it's that taste and persistence compound. Raw speed doesn't necessarily.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t describe my trajectory as a straight line where I was always the strongest student and knew exactly what to do next. When you compare yourself with the highest-achieving students, it’s easy to focus on how early they seemed to figure things out. But I think the more useful question is whether you’re gradually finding problems you care about and developing the ability to work on them independently.

For me, that’s how I’d think about an academic trajectory: less as a ranking and more as a process of finding direction. Being good at solving a problem someone gives you is valuable. Learning to decide which problem is worth pursuing is a different skill, and people develop that at different speeds.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t really see my path as a straight line where I was always the best student and then naturally became a researcher. Compared with the highest-achieving students, I think my trajectory has been more about gradually figuring out what interests me and where I can contribute.

Of course, when you see people who seem to be ahead at every stage, you compare yourself with them. But doing research is different from taking exams. There isn’t a fixed set of questions with a known answer. You have to find a question you care about, develop your own judgment, and keep working when you don’t know whether an idea will succeed.

So I try to think less about whether I’m ahead of someone else and more about whether I’m becoming better at asking questions and pursuing them independently. That’s a more useful way for me to understand my trajectory.
